This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. slides.title: 2.1.1 Interpreting Big-O Notation
keyPoints: A linear scan can examine every one of n elements, giving O(n) comparisons in its worst case.
A lower-bound search on an indexed sorted sequence halves an interval, giving O(log n) comparisons.
A nested all-pairs loop often produces O(n squared), while a constant amount of work independent of n is O(1).
Constants and lower-order terms are suppressed in these growth descriptions, not declared irrelevant to real.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 2, treat 2.1.1 Interpreting Big-O Notation as an algorithmic claim. A linear scan can examine every one of n elements, giving O(n) comparisons in its worst case. A lower-bound search on an indexed sorted sequence halves an interval, giving O(log n) comparisons. A nested all-pairs loop often produces O(n squared), while a constant amount of work independent of n is O(1). Constants and lower-order terms are suppressed in these growth descriptions, not declared irrelevant to real systems. An O(n) method can be faster for a small dataset than an O(log n) method with expensive setup. The analysis answers scaling questions; measurement answers a particular implementation question over a particular workload. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: Failure clinic — A valid measurement answering the wrong question
keyPoints: A colleague claims binary search is always better because its comparison count is lower.

Sorting a fresh collection for a single query can cost more total work than one scan.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 2, treat Failure clinic — A valid measurement answering the wrong question as an algorithmic claim. A colleague claims binary search is always better because its comparison count is lower. Ask who paid to sort the input and how many searches will reuse that order. Sorting a fresh collection for a single query can cost more total work than one scan. For a static collection queried repeatedly, preprocessing may be justified. The correct comparison is between complete workflows with the same contract. Another report divides a single elapsed time by n and labels the quotient the cost per element. If the timed region contains allocation, startup, parsing, and output, the quotient is not solely an element-processing cost. It may still be a useful end-to-end measure, but it needs the correct name. Do not remove inconvenient overhead from one implementation while retaining it for its competitor. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 2, treat Guided lab — Build an operation ledger as an algorithmic claim. Extend the counting program in a separate project to print rows for sizes zero, one, two, four, eight, sixteen, and 1024. For linear search, include first match, last match, and absence. For binary lower-bound counting, include keys below the range, inside it, and above it. Do not dereference a search result merely to count comparisons. Add a second growth simulation that expands by one. For ten appends, the relocation count should be the sum zero through nine, which is 45. For doubling growth, compute the actual count from capacity boundaries. Compare cumulative movement, maximum movement in one append, and unused capacity. These three measures expose different tradeoffs. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
